extracted.intended_audience: news reporters, editors, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on producing and evaluating newspaper and television news stories, including source selection, factual verification, narrative form (hard vs. soft news), labeling, and visual/film conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradation of sources / centralized sources
rubrics_metrics.description: News reports draw heavily upon police versions and other centralized, legitimated officials (police, university PR officers, union heads, industry spokespeople) rather than ordinary citizens or rank-and-file participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: riot coverage privileging police accounts, student strike counts taken from university officials, union effectiveness estimated from union heads. This gradation legitimates certain truth-claims and marginalizes less institutional voices; journalists rely on those sources because they are part of the news net and perceived as authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious use of quotation marks to distance reporter
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks are used as a technical device to distance the reporter from statements and to convert others' opinions into mutually self-validating facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations allow reporters to present opinions without appearing to editorialize; they can signal 'so-called' (e.g., the 'New Left') and protect against managerial criticism. Anti-pattern: using unattributed or thinly sourced quotations to mask a reporter's own view or to evade verification, or piling on quotations without corroborating facts (which can risk libel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow legal procedural sequencing unless convinced of miscarriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers should follow the legal steps as they appear in an arrest–indictment–trial sequence unless convinced there has been a miscarriage of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may reject or delay stories that preempt legal processes; only when convinced of serious injustice should a paper 'pull out all the stops and crusade for the accused.' This standard protects newspapers from appearing to judge prematurely and from libel exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require sufficient facts / verification before running a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories containing too many unanswered questions should be withheld until additional facts are obtained; reporters/editors must seek supplementary evidence to claim objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: checking medical treatment, determining causal connections, calling police and other sources. Editors want 'more facts' to counter inferences about procedures (e.g., police 'clamming up' implies possible arrest). Lack of corroboration can make a story libelous or professionally indefensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label interpretive material explicitly (e.g., 'news analysis', 'commentary')
rubrics_metrics.description: Material that is interpretive or opinionated should be set off with distinct formal labels to indicate it is not straightforward factual reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels like 'news analysis' or 'commentary' place a barrier between problematic/interpretive stories and routine factual pieces, protecting the organization's claim to factuality for unlabeled items and signaling to readers/viewers to weigh the reporter's qualifications and prior work when assessing the interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hard news (fact) from soft news (feature) in presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news is equated with 'facts' and a lead-documentation mode; soft news or features employ varied narrative devices and are more openly interpretive or literary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard-news stories lead with who/what/where/when/why/how and follow inverted-pyramid or block documentation; soft-news pieces may use hooks, unattributed quotations, surprise endings, or multiple narrators. Features often require special editorial care and different professional skills; they are treated as exceptions to the standard facticity mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inverted-pyramid and block styles to claim facticity and enable editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard story structures (lead followed by documentation in decreasing order, or block style with leads followed by supporting facts) are professional devices that present facticity and allow editors to trim copy from the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These forms are taught in journalism texts and enable both factual claim-making and practical newsroom operations (space/length editing). Alternative structures can be professional if they maintain the web of facticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness criteria: prominence, public warning, and frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of which deaths/events become lead news depends on factors like prominence (e.g., governor's grandchild), capacity to serve as public warning (e.g., tenement child), and the narrative frame used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters ask with whom colleagues spoke and why information appears; frames guide which facts are sought and which sources are used. This selection process is normative for newswork and shapes which events become news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use known story forms to guide fact-finding (e.g., 'the fire', 'the trial')
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepted story typologies (fires, trials, conventions, lost child, etc.) guide reporters about which facts to seek and which centralized sources to consult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These forms reduce idiosyncrasy and provide routinized questions and sources, helping reporters work quickly and predictably. Anti-pattern: reliance on forms can lead to missed or wrong conclusions when events deviate from expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional skill: building narratives while preserving facticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionalism includes the ability to craft narratives (even by bending or breaking rules) that nonetheless maintain the web of facticity and organizational standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: creative leads that 'back into' the inverted pyramid, minimal editing preferred by some reporters, editors' pride in reworking copy. Professionalism also involves adherence to the organization's stylebook when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to organizational style and the newsroom's formal conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the organization's style (often formalized in a style book) is a professional requirement; it shapes grammar, vocabulary, and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style conformity supports the newsroom's claim to professionalism and ensures consistent readable copy. Editors may edit for adherence and to locate unanswered questions. Some reporters prize autonomy; editors prize reworking copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newswriting language conventions (tense, sentence length, paragraph length)
rubrics_metrics.description: News prose conventions: stories in past tense, headlines in present; paragraphs short (1–3 sentences); sentences generally under ~20 words; avoid long polysyllabic words; prefer inverted word order typical of news-speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These linguistic rules aim to increase clarity and perceived facticity. The text warns of 'news-speak' (awkward lengthy constructions and hackneyed transitions) and notes that contemporary conventions have evolved (shorter leads, lighter pages) to suit readers and competing media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize undocumented value judgments in factual pages
rubrics_metrics.description: News analysis implies value judgments; straight news is expected to have 'no value judgments whatsoever'—editors are alert to the 'number and degree of value judgments undocumented at the time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and editors rely on professional instincts and source reliability to judge whether an item is unduly loaded. When value judgments are present without documentation, labeling as analysis or withholding is appropriate to maintain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate representativeness of sources and symbolic treatment of interviewees
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should assess whether interviewed sources are truly representative (e.g., workers sometimes interviewed only as 'symbols') and be aware that official sources may have self-interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overreliance on official spokespersons for estimates or interpretations when they have clear biases; seek a range of sources where representativeness matters for the story's claim to facticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal segmentation and scheduling (sections, slots, labels) as editorial controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers and broadcasts use sections, pages, scheduled time slots, and labels (op-ed, sports, weather, 'kicker', 'news analysis') to structure content and signal mode (factual vs interpretive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement and labels both reflect and enforce the web of facticity: certain kinds of material are expected in certain slots, and labels protect the organization's factual claims elsewhere. Program timing (recurring features) also constrains and standardizes content.

rubrics_metrics.name: News film grammar and the claim to 'actuality'
rubrics_metrics.description: Television news film presents itself as 'actuality' and claims neutrality by appearing not to manipulate time/space; however, film is governed by conventions (frame composition, rhythm, shot selection) that constitute a visual language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters/cameramen must follow explicit visual rules (e.g., avoid inappropriate fast/slow motion that undermines credibility). Exceptions exist (sports use slow motion). Analysts and practitioners should avoid the 'representational temptation'—assuming pictures are simple windows onto reality—because film choices shape meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain proper temporal/spatial rendition in film (avoid distorted frame rates/tempo)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rhythm of film (frames per second, pacing) must not introduce unintended effects; inappropriate fast or slow motion can impugn a news organization's credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When film rhythm cannot be corrected in projection, footage may be discarded. Exceptions: sports or other labeled segments where slow-motion or altered tempo serves a legitimate informational function (e.g., judging a play).
